text:
Artificial intelligence is changing how educational institutions assess student performance. Traditional assessment often depends on examinations, essays, and teacher-led marking. AI-supported systems can now analyse responses, identify learning patterns, and provide rapid feedback. Although these tools may improve efficiency, they also raise concerns about fairness, transparency, and the quality of evaluation.

One important benefit of AI is faster assessment. Automated systems can mark multiple-choice tests, grammar exercises, and structured responses within seconds. This allows students to receive immediate feedback rather than waiting several days or weeks. Teachers can also use assessment data to identify common misunderstandings and adjust their lessons accordingly.

AI may also support continuous assessment. Instead of evaluating students only through major examinations, digital platforms can monitor progress across quizzes, exercises, and learning activities. This approach may provide a more complete picture of student development. It can also help teachers identify students who require additional support before they fail an important assessment.

However, automated assessment has limitations. AI can evaluate measurable features such as accuracy, structure, and language patterns, but it may struggle to recognise creativity, originality, cultural context, or unusual but valid reasoning. Students may also be disadvantaged when evaluation systems are trained on narrow examples of acceptable responses.

Transparency is therefore essential. Students and teachers should understand how automated scores are produced and how those scores influence academic decisions. Human review must remain available when results are disputed or when the assessment has serious consequences.

AI can make assessment faster, more consistent, and more informative. Nevertheless, it should not become the sole authority in evaluating student ability. The most effective approach combines automated analysis with human judgement, ensuring that assessment remains efficient without becoming narrow or unfair.
